Apple and other tech giants could be forced to make annual lump-sum payments to the EU under a revised digital services tax proposal.

The EU is hoping to amend an earlier plan in a way that raises revenue without drawing the ire of the White House...

EU member states have long argued over digital services taxes, with Apple — whose services include iCloud, Apple Music, Apple TV, Apple Creator Studio, and more — frequently cited as an example.

Some argue these companies earn massive revenues from subscription services sold to EU citizens without paying tax on those earnings in Europe. Others worry a digital tax could disproportionately affect European businesses, and some fear the White House will threaten retaliation if U.S. companies are taxed more heavily.

The European Commission has now proposed a compromise designed to please everyone — except Apple, Google, and Meta, which would be the ones paying the new tax, according to the Financial Times.

Officials say Brussels is considering modifying an existing plan to require all companies operating in the EU with annual revenues above €100 million to pay a flat annual fee. The idea is that by adjusting the thresholds and contribution levels of the Core proposal so it only applies to very large companies, Brussels can increase the tax take from tech groups while defusing European criticism that the Core plan would sweep in many mid-sized European companies.

The revised plan would not single out companies that sell digital services, but would apply to all large companies. Since it was the earlier plan that prompted the White House to threaten retaliatory tariffs, the EU hopes this version won't reignite a trade war with the U.S.

The amount each company would be charged has not yet been decided. The plan is to first reach agreement on the principle among the EU's 27 member states, and then settle on the rate.

9to5Mac Take

This mess should have been resolved by a globally agreed deal brokered by the OECD. Such a deal would ensure that all companies around the world pay at least some tax in each of the countries where they operate — and Apple has said it supports it.

But Donald Trump pulled the U.S. out of the deal, leading to calls within the EU for an EU-only version. Assuming Trump won't object to a revised plan strikes me as optimistic.
